newsitem.title: ITALY: TENNIS-BECKER'S CAREER WILL END AT THE SCHOOL GATE.
newsitem.headline: TENNIS-BECKER'S CAREER WILL END AT THE SCHOOL GATE.

text.p: Former Wimbledon champion Boris Becker, said on Tuesday his son's education could interfere with his tennis in the future.
"It depends on so many things," the German replied when asked at the Italian Open whether he intended to retire professionally in three years' time.
"My son has to go to school and then I cannot travel every week like I am doing now," said Becker, whose son Noah was three years old in January.
Then, smiling, he suggested a way ahead.
"But maybe I can still play in the holidays and go to Wimbledon in the summer. You have to play when you can."
Becker, who won the Australian Open in 1991 and 1996 and the U.S. Open in 1990 as well s three Wimbledon titles, said that motivation was not a problem and neither was fitness.
"I'm still at an age where I can do it," he said when asked if he had any motivational difficulties after winning so much and with many of his great former foes now retired.
"Playing tennis is something I truly like to do. That's why I do it. Its easy."

"Physically I feel 100 percent. My wrist injury did not stop me from going to the gym or from running a lot," the 29-year-old said after beating Italian Andrea Gaudenzi 7-6 6-2 in his first round match on the red clay of the Foro Italico.
Becker has been plagued by injury and had a two-month break this year due to tendinitis in his right wrist.
He crashed out of the Monte Carlo Open to Italy's Renzo Furlan in the first round in his comeback last month and the Rome tournament is only his sixth of the year.
In his most recent tournament in Hamburg, the German who has never won a claycourt title reached the third round where he lost to Spain's Felix Mantilla.
Gaudenzi took Becker to a tie-break in the first set, losing 7-3, but Becker dispelled any creeping notion that the crowd might have had that their man could cause an upset.
He led the second set 4-0, with serves crashing in at more than 200 kph, before Gaudenzi managed to hold serve.
"I don't remember when I last played four games like those in the second set," Becker said. "They were perfect."
The fans, despite occasional whistles as Becker served, appeared evenly divided between the two men in a sign of the German's popularity and how much he will be missed.
Few other players could divide one of the most notoriously partisan crowds in tennis as Becker did.
"It's good to know when there's a crisis on centre court that 50 percent of the crowd want you to do well," he said.
